title: have
subtitle: I've got / I have / I had
summary: Use have and have got to say what is yours, and use have (never have got) in expressions like have breakfast, have a shower and have a good time.

lesson.heading: have and have got
lesson.text: **I've got** something and **I have** something mean the same thing: it is mine. Both are correct, so you can choose.

examples.text: I**'ve got** a new car. *or* I **have** a new car.
Sue **has got** long hair. *or* Sue **has** long hair.
**Have** they **got** any children? *or* **Do** they **have** any children?
Tim **hasn't got** a job. *or* Tim **doesn't have** a job.
How much time **have** you **got**? *or* How much time **do** you **have**?

lesson.heading: Illnesses
lesson.text: We use **have got** or **have** for illnesses too: a headache, a toothache, a pain in my leg, a cold, a cough, a sore throat, a temperature, flu.

examples.text: I**'ve got** a headache. *or* I **have** a headache.
**Have** you **got** a cold? *or* **Do** you **have** a cold?

lesson.heading: The past: I had
lesson.text: In the past we say **I had** (with no *got*), **I didn't have** and **Did you have?**

examples.text: When I first met Sue, she **had** short hair.
He **didn't have** any money because he **didn't have** a job.
**Did** you **have** enough time to do everything you wanted?

lesson.heading: have breakfast / have a cup of coffee
rows: breakfast / lunch / dinner
*A:* Where's Liz? *B:* She**'s having** lunch.
a meal / a sandwich / a pizza
I **don't** usually **have** breakfast.
a cup of coffee / a glass of milk
I **had** three cups of coffee this morning.
something to eat / something to drink
*A:* **Have** a biscuit! *B:* Oh, thank you.
lesson.note: In these expressions **have** = eat, drink or take. You cannot use *have got* here.

lesson.heading: More expressions with have
rows: a bath / a shower
I **had** a shower this morning.
a rest / a holiday / a party
We**'re having** a party next week. You must come.
a nice time / a good trip / fun
Enjoy your holiday. **Have** a nice time!
a walk / a swim / a game (of tennis)
**Did** you **have** a good time in Tokyo?
a dream / an accident / a baby
Sandra **has** just **had** a baby.
a look (at something)
Can I **have** a look at your newspaper?

lesson.heading: have got or have?

left.label: have got or have (= it is mine)
left.text: A man points at a new shower in his bathroom.
examples: I**'ve got** a new shower. It's very good.
I **have** a new shower. It's very good.

right.label: have only (not have got)
right.text: A woman is under the water in the shower now.
examples: *A:* Where's Paul? *B:* He**'s having** a shower.

lesson.note: Not ~~I've got a shower every morning~~. Here *have* = take, so *have got* is not possible.

exercises.prompt: He can't open the door. He ___ a key.
exercises.explanation: He hasn't got a key or He doesn't have a key. Both are correct.

exercises.prompt: ___ a cold last week. He's better now.
exercises.explanation: Last week is the past, so we use had (with no got).

exercises.prompt: ___ any problems when you were on holiday?
exercises.explanation: The holiday is finished, so the past question is Did you have ... ?

exercises.prompt: We wanted to go by taxi, but ___ enough money.
exercises.explanation: The past negative is didn't have.

exercises.prompt: Liz is very busy. ___ much free time.
exercises.explanation: She hasn't got much free time or She doesn't have much free time.

exercises.prompt: Can you use have got here, or do you need have only?
What are these people doing? Match each situation with the right sentence.

pairs.left: A woman is sitting down with a teapot and a cup.
pairs.right: She's having a cup of tea.

pairs.left: A man is lying on the sofa with his eyes closed.
A family are round the table in the morning with bread and coffee.
An old couple are eating at a table in the evening.
A man is sitting in the bath in a lot of water.
People are laughing on a fast ride at the fair.

exercises.prompt: Emily is going on holiday. What do you say to her before she goes? ___ a nice holiday!
exercises.explanation: Have a nice holiday! We use have for a nice time, a good trip and so on.

exercises.prompt: It's Monday morning. You are at work. Ask Paula about her weekend: ___ a nice weekend?
exercises.explanation: The weekend is finished, so we ask Did you have a nice weekend?

exercises.prompt: *A:* Shall we ___? *B:* No, I'm not hungry.
exercises.explanation: Here have = eat, so have got is not possible.

exercises.statement: I've got a shower every morning.
exercises.explanation: I have a shower every morning. Here have = take, so have got is not possible.

exercises.prompt: Put the question in the right order.
exercises.answer: Did you have enough time to do everything you wanted?
exercises.explanation: In past questions we use did + have, not had.
